newsitem.title: USA: US sugar group bracing for House attack on program.
newsitem.headline: US sugar group bracing for House attack on program.

text.p: The U.S. sugar program, which Congress last dealt with in the 1996 farm bill, could come under attack again in the coming weeks, congressional aides and sugar industry lobbyists said.
"We're bracing for any eventuality," Jack Roney, director of economics and policy analysis for the American Sugar Alliance, told Reuters.
On Wednesday, the House Appropriations subcommittee on agriculture will take up legislation to provide funding for U.S. Agriculture Department programs in fiscal 1998 (September-October).
While an attack on the program is possible at that stage, opponents will probably wait until the spending bill reaches the full committee or the House floor, Roney said.

Unlike other farm programs, the sugar program does not provide a direct government payment to producers. However, critics charge that it boosts consumer costs by supporting U.S. sugar prices above world levels.

Congress made some changes to the program in the 1996 farm bill, but left an annual import quota and price support loan largely intact. Growers say they need those provisions to shield them from unfair foreign competition.
Earlier this year, Reps. Charles Schumer, a New York Democrat, and Dan Miller, a Florida Republican, introduced legislation to phase out the sugar program by 2003.

Miller told reporters he saw a "reasonable" chance the bill would be approved. However, the U.S. sugar industry has had several months since then to lobby against the bill, which they say would immediately gut the program.
Miller is a member of the full House Appropriations Committee, but not the subcommittee on agriculture.
As of Monday, Miller was still considering "several possible" sugar amendments that he could offer during full committee consideration or when the bill reaches the House floor, a spokeswoman said.
One past sugar program opponent who does serve on the agriculture appropriations subcommittee is Rep. Jack Kingston, a Georgia Republican.
However, Kingston does not plan to go after the program during the subcommittee markup, a spokeswoman said.
Kingston is satisfied with expected language in the spending bill that would require USDA to report twice a year on the operation of the sugar program, the spokeswoman said.
Similar language accompanied the fiscal 1997 agricultural appropriations bill and was acceptable to sugar growers.
